task.goal: Reduce missed updates in a volunteer-run community calendar where events arrive by email and printed flyers.
hard_constraints: Three volunteers share a free spreadsheet and have no authority to change senders' habits.
No event may be published without date, place and source confirmation; corrections must be traceable.
Keep weekly upkeep under two hours and avoid collecting attendee names.
task.available_resources: Existing inbox, flyer tray and a static public calendar page.
task.expected_result: A low-maintenance intake and verification process with an error audit.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One shared verification queue with explicit handoffs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make every incoming event a spreadsheet row before anyone edits the public calendar. The main mechanism is a visible queue: incomplete items remain assigned and visible instead of disappearing in an inbox or flyer pile. Use columns for event ID, intake date, title, event date/time, place, source reference, confirmation evidence, owner, status and last action. Statuses are Needs confirmation, Ready, Published and Cancelled. The source reference is an email subject/date or an ID written on a retained flyer; avoid copying attendee names or entire email threads.

Rotate three roles weekly: intake, verification and publication/audit. Intake scans new mail and the flyer tray, checks for duplicates and records events. Verification checks the original source for explicit date and place. If either is ambiguous, request clarification through the existing inbox; silence does not count as confirmation. Publication accepts only Ready rows with all three requirements recorded. The original sender's clear written announcement or an attributable flyer can serve as confirmation, assuming that meets the community's policy; otherwise obtain organizer confirmation before publishing.

Record corrections in an append-only spreadsheet tab with event ID, old value, new value, evidence, volunteer and timestamp. Update the page, then record completion. Retain superseded source evidence through the audit period.

Budget 35 minutes for intake, 35 for verification and clarification, 25 for publication and 15 for audit: 110 volunteer-minutes total each week. This assumes modest volume and simple page editing. When time runs out, leave unresolved items unpublished and visibly queued. The limit is that a missed initial capture remains invisible; the audit must therefore sample original inputs as well as rows.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, operate the queue and compare its output with a brief independent scan using the current informal method. Count this comparison within the 110-minute budget. Audit five original inputs and five published entries each week, or all if fewer. Check capture, confirmed date/place/source, and page agreement. Log omissions and incorrect fields with corrective actions. The mechanism is challenged if the informal scan finds eligible events the queue missed, if any published entry lacks evidence, or if total upkeep reaches two hours. This small check can reveal failures but cannot establish a reliable long-term error rate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reconcile each source batch directly against the public page
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use regular source-to-page reconciliation rather than a continuously managed workflow. The main mechanism is coverage accounting: every email or flyer in a bounded batch must have a recorded disposition, and every public entry must point back to confirmed evidence. This can catch omissions even when volunteers forget to create an event row.

Twice weekly, one volunteer reviews all inbox messages since the previous recorded cutoff, including older threads with new replies, and every flyer newly placed in the tray. Give flyers sequential IDs and retain them in reviewed and unreviewed sections. Record each relevant source in a free spreadsheet with its reference, event ID, date, place, confirmation evidence and disposition: Published, Duplicate, Awaiting clarification, Cancelled or Not an event. Record batch boundaries and completion time. Do not delete processed sources during the audit period.

A second volunteer compares the batch with the static page and applies verified additions or corrections. Publication requires explicit date, place and attributable source confirmation; ambiguous material stays unpublished while clarification is requested through the inbox. A third volunteer performs a small reverse audit from page entries back to evidence and checks unresolved items. Rotate duties weekly. Maintain an append-only corrections tab containing old and new values, source evidence, timestamp and editor; record when each page correction is complete. Store event information only, without attendee lists.

Allocate two 35-minute reconciliation sessions, 25 minutes for clarification and page changes, and 15 minutes for audit: 110 volunteer-minutes weekly. This assumes manageable input volume, recoverable inbox history and cheap page edits. Its advantage is explicit coverage of source batches; its limits are publication delay between sessions and vulnerability to an incorrectly defined cutoff. If input exceeds capacity, record the unfinished boundary and resume there rather than marking the batch complete.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot four batches. Within the audit allowance, have the auditor independently rescan one completed batch before viewing its dispositions, then compare eligible events and corrections found. Use the current informal inbox-and-tray scan as the simple comparator on that same batch. Also trace five public entries to evidence and inspect all pending items for accidental publication. Record omissions, unsupported entries, correction mismatches and total volunteer-minutes. A supposedly completed batch containing an undispositioned event falsifies its coverage claim. Missing confirmation or upkeep reaching two hours shows the implementation needs simplification or a lower supported volume; four batches provide only preliminary evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Give each event a recheck deadline and expire stale information
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use scheduled revalidation to catch changes before an event occurs. The main mechanism is a time-limited confirmation: an event's initial announcement does not remain sufficient indefinitely. This targets postponed, relocated or cancelled events whose updates might otherwise remain buried in email.

In the shared spreadsheet, record event ID, title, date/time, place, original source reference, confirmation evidence, last checked date, next check date and public-page status. Twice weekly, one volunteer captures new events from the inbox and flyer tray. Publish only when date, place and an attributable source are explicitly confirmed. A clear organizer email or attributable flyer may qualify if community policy accepts it; ambiguity requires clarification through the existing inbox.

Assign each published event one recheck shortly before it occurs, allowing time for a response. A second volunteer searches the existing inbox for later messages about due events and checks retained flyers for replacements. If necessary, contact the organizer using an existing source contact. Silence is not renewed confirmation. When confirmation expires, remove the event from the public page until reconfirmed. This deliberately trades some calendar completeness for fewer stale listings.

A third volunteer handles page changes and audits. Record every correction or removal in an append-only spreadsheet tab with event ID, previous value, replacement value, evidence reference, editor, timestamp and page-update completion. Retain referenced emails and numbered flyers; collect no attendee names.

Budget 30 minutes for intake, 40 for rechecks and clarification, 25 for page changes and 15 for audit: 110 total volunteer-minutes weekly. This requires modest event volume, inexpensive page editing and acceptance of temporary removals. It cannot detect uncommunicated changes without organizer responses, and revalidation may become costly at higher volume.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot for two weeks, counting audit and comparison work within the budget. Select five events due for recheck, or all if fewer. First record what an ordinary scan of newly arrived email and flyers would change; then perform the scheduled event-specific searches and clarification. Compare evidence-backed corrections discovered and time spent. Independently inspect five original inputs for missed intake and trace five public entries to current date, place and source evidence. Inspect the correction history against the page. The mechanism fails its operating requirements if an expired event remains published, an entry lacks required confirmation, or total upkeep reaches two hours. If rechecks repeatedly find no additional changes while causing substantial removals or backlog, they may offer insufficient benefit over the simple scan. Two weeks cannot establish a reliable error rate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Independent discovery passes with a disagreement check
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use two independent, brief discovery passes to reduce dependence on one volunteer noticing every relevant message or flyer. The main mechanism is redundant detection: volunteers record what they find before seeing each other's findings, then investigate disagreements. This differs from assigning intake to one person because a second reader can catch an omission before publication.

Twice weekly, two volunteers independently inspect email received since the previous session and flyers added to a designated section of the existing tray. Include replies in older email threads. Each records a short source reference and whether it announces an event, changes an existing event or needs investigation, using separate spreadsheet tabs. Number flyers so both readers can identify the same item. Keep reviewed flyers available until reconciliation finishes.

The third volunteer compares the two lists, investigates unmatched findings and maintains the event records and public page. An item found by only one reader still receives full consideration; agreement between readers is not proof of accuracy. Publication requires explicit date, place and attributable source evidence. Assume a clear organizer email or attributable flyer can provide that evidence; otherwise request confirmation through the existing inbox and keep the event unpublished pending a reply.

For corrections, append the event ID, previous and replacement values, evidence reference, editor, timestamp and page-update completion to a history tab. Retain the referenced sources. Record event details only, without attendee names.

Allow each reader 15 minutes per session, the reconciler 35 minutes weekly, and an independent error audit 15 minutes: 110 total volunteer-minutes. Rotate roles weekly. This requires low enough volume for two short passes and straightforward page editing. Shared blind spots remain possible, and unfinished material must stay visibly pending rather than being treated as reviewed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot for two weeks. Preserve the first reader's findings as the simple single-reader comparator, then count additional valid events or corrections contributed by the second reader. Within the audit allowance, inspect three original inputs absent from both lists and trace three public entries to date, place and source evidence; inspect any correction against its history and the page. Log omissions, unsupported publication, mismatched corrections and total time. An unsupported entry violates the publication rule; reaching 120 volunteer-minutes violates the upkeep limit. If the second pass adds no useful discoveries while delaying processing, its extra cost is not justified by this pilot. A small sample cannot establish a dependable miss rate.

EXPAND.title: Generate the public calendar from confirmed spreadsheet records
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the spreadsheet the sole editable event record and generate the static page from it. The main mechanism is eliminating separate editing of spreadsheet records and public listings: a confirmed correction changes the next page output automatically. This targets transcription errors, forgotten page corrections and differences between volunteers’ copies. It does not depend on volunteers maintaining two matching representations.

Use one sheet for event ID, title, date/time, place, source reference, confirmation evidence and publication status. Retain referenced emails and number retained flyers. A clear, attributable announcement can establish confirmation if the community accepts it; otherwise request clarification through the existing inbox. Missing or ambiguous date, place or source confirmation blocks publication. Collect event information only, without attendee names.

A protected output tab uses spreadsheet formulas to produce chronologically ordered HTML from eligible records, including stable event IDs. One volunteer copies that output into the existing static page. Escape special characters and exclude internal evidence and contact details from public output. The other volunteers capture inputs and verify evidence; rotate these duties. Before changing a confirmed record, append its old and new values, evidence reference, editor and timestamp to a corrections tab. Record the page release time against included corrections so pending publication remains visible.

Allow 35 minutes for intake, 35 for verification, 20 for generation and publication, and 20 for audit: 110 total volunteer-minutes weekly. Setup requires someone comfortable with spreadsheet formulas and access to replace the page’s event section. This assumes modest volume and that the static page accepts generated HTML. Audit both a small sample of original inputs against records and public entries against evidence. Excess work stays visibly pending and unpublished. Generation reduces copying mistakes but cannot establish source truth or recover an input nobody captured.
EXPAND.experiment: Build a small unpublished output using existing examples or explicitly synthetic records: one complete event, one missing a place, one lacking source confirmation, one correction and a title containing special characters. Compare it with manually editing the same entries. Reject or revise the approach if an incomplete record appears, internal evidence leaks, a correction fails to propagate, or HTML breaks. Then time one live weekly cycle, including audit; exceeding 120 total volunteer-minutes would falsify the upkeep assumption at that volume.

REFINE.title: Repair candidate 1: distinguish repeat notices from event updates
REFINE.proposal: Original candidate 1 is the strongest fit: bounded source-to-page reconciliation makes missed intake visible using the existing tools. Its specific weakness is the undefined Duplicate disposition: a later email or replacement flyer about an existing event could be dismissed as a duplicate even when it changes the date, place or cancellation status. Change one action: before marking a source Duplicate, compare its date, place and event status with the linked event row. Only matching information qualifies as a duplicate. Differences or conflicting claims receive an Update awaiting verification disposition linked to that event; they prevent batch completion until recorded and assigned, but need not be resolved before completion. Apply verified changes through the existing correction log and page-update process. If conflicting evidence undermines the published date or place, temporarily unpublish the entry and log that action until resolved. Publication still requires explicit date, place and attributable source confirmation. Prerequisites are retained sources and enough event identity information to link notices; uncertain matches remain pending. Keep the existing 110 volunteer-minute weekly budget, including comparisons, and collect no attendee names. The remaining limit is that unreceived changes cannot be detected, and ambiguous notices may remain unresolved.
REFINE.experiment: Within the existing audit allowance, walk through three mock sources for one published event: an identical repeat, a changed venue and an ambiguous postponement. The repeat should become Duplicate; the changed venue should produce a linked, evidence-backed correction and matching page update; the ambiguous postponement should remain pending with a traceable temporary removal. The repair is falsified if either changed notice is discarded as Duplicate, an unsupported event remains published, or a page change lacks correction history. Count the exercise within the weekly budget.

First record what an ordinary scan of newly arrived email and flyers would change; then perform the scheduled event-specific searches and clarification. Compare evidence-backed corrections discovered and time spent. Independently inspect five original inputs for missed intake and trace five public entries to current date, place and source evidence. Inspect the correction history against the page. The mechanism fails its operating requirements if an expired event remains published, an entry lacks required confirmation, or total upkeep reaches two hours. If rechecks repeatedly find no additional changes while causing substantial removals or backlog, they may offer insufficient benefit over the simple scan. Two weeks cannot establish a reliable error rate.

SAVE.title: Independent discovery passes with a disagreement check
SAVE.proposal:
Use two independent, brief discovery passes to reduce dependence on one volunteer noticing every relevant message or flyer. The main mechanism is redundant detection: volunteers record what they find before seeing each other's findings, then investigate disagreements. This differs from assigning intake to one person because a second reader can catch an omission before publication.

Twice weekly, two volunteers independently inspect email received since the previous session and flyers added to a designated section of the existing tray. Include replies in older email threads. Each records a short source reference and whether it announces an event, changes an existing event or needs investigation, using separate spreadsheet tabs. Number flyers so both readers can identify the same item. Keep reviewed flyers available until reconciliation finishes.

The third volunteer compares the two lists, investigates unmatched findings and maintains the event records and public page. An item found by only one reader still receives full consideration; agreement between readers is not proof of accuracy. Publication requires explicit date, place and attributable source evidence. Assume a clear organizer email or attributable flyer can provide that evidence; otherwise request confirmation through the existing inbox and keep the event unpublished pending a reply.

For corrections, append the event ID, previous and replacement values, evidence reference, editor, timestamp and page-update completion to a history tab. Retain the referenced sources. Record event details only, without attendee names.

Allow each reader 15 minutes per session, the reconciler 35 minutes weekly, and an independent error audit 15 minutes: 110 total volunteer-minutes. Rotate roles weekly. This requires low enough volume for two short passes and straightforward page editing. Shared blind spots remain possible, and unfinished material must stay visibly pending rather than being treated as reviewed.
SAVE.experiment: Pilot for two weeks. Preserve the first reader's findings as the simple single-reader comparator, then count additional valid events or corrections contributed by the second reader. Within the audit allowance, inspect three original inputs absent from both lists and trace three public entries to date, place and source evidence; inspect any correction against its history and the page. Log omissions, unsupported publication, mismatched corrections and total time. An unsupported entry violates the publication rule; reaching 120 volunteer-minutes violates the upkeep limit. If the second pass adds no useful discoveries while delaying processing, its extra cost is not justified by this pilot. A small sample cannot establish a dependable miss rate.
